c0006: Average number of events you cater per year, counting every drop-off, backyard paella party, wedding, corporate booking and premium seafood event. It is the main volume driver of the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, and years 2 and 3 grow in events. The example is a full-time owner-paella chef with a second cook on weekends, not the average first year. Compare it with the capacity row further down.
c0008: EXCL. sales tax, with the paella chef, the staff and the service charge included and the voluntary gratuity left out: the blended price per guest across everything you sell, not the price of any one package. Price per guest incl. sales tax = this value × (1 + your sales tax rate). Operators quote per person (live paella with salad and bread, or a full Spanish menu with staff); the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab shows the ranges. The Pricing Calculator quotes three packages per guest: to bring them here, add the service charge you keep to each package subtotal, divide by its billable guests, then weight each package's price by the guests you expect to serve with it in a year.
c0010: Average number of guests per event across your whole mix, from drop-off lunches for a few dozen people to weddings of well over a hundred. Operators set guest minimums (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab). Sales per event = guests × price per guest. One cell for the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, so they always agree.
c0012: Growth in events in year 2 over year 1 (enter 0.10 for 10%). Kept conservative on purpose: reviews and wedding bookings build up months ahead, and one paella chef with one van limits how fast you can grow.
c0014: Growth in events in year 3 over year 2, kept conservative for the same reason: repeat corporate clients and planner referrals build up slowly, and one van and one paella chef limit the weekends you can sell.
c0018: Share of sales that comes from paella packages: the live-cooked paella with salad and bread, plus the paella chef and the staff who serve it. It is an INPUT: change it here and the P&L, the cash flow and the sales tax collected recalculate on their own. The rest of your sales are add-ons.
c0020: Calculated as the remainder: paella packages + add-ons = 100%. Add-ons are tapas hour, desserts, non-alcoholic sangria and drinks, rentals, extra hours and travel fees.
c0022: Cost of goods sold on paella package sales: bomba rice, seafood, chicken and chorizo, saffron, stock, salad and bread, with a cushion for overproduction and for volatile seafood prices. The example sits inside the 28-35% food cost range for caterers in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab. Seafood prices swing, so it is the most sensitive lever in the plan: test it at the top of the range before you trust the result.
c0024: Cost of goods sold on add-ons: tapas ingredients, bought-in desserts and the rentals you pass on at close to cost. There is no alcohol in this line: the client buys it separately, and sangria goes out without alcohol.
c0026: Disposables and cooking fuel as a % of sales: plates, cutlery, napkins and foil pans, plus the propane that fires the burners at every event (about 6-8 lb, or 2.7-3.6 kg, for a 60-guest event: Kit estimate) and wood only where a permit allows it. It scales with the number of events and the pans you cook. Van fuel is NOT here: it has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab. Some cities restrict foam and single-use plastics, so check your local rules.
c0032: Card and ACH fees on total sales. Private clients pay their deposit and balance by card; many companies pay by ACH or check, which lowers the cost. The example is a blended rate: a percentage plus a per-transaction fee, which weighs more on small invoices. Check your processor's statement and enter your effective rate (Kit estimate).
c0042: Monthly cost of your commissary kitchen (hours + storage) and the space for your paella pans and burners: one cell for everything you pay the commissary. Pick a kitchen that lets you store burners and propane cylinders, and ask the health department and the fire marshal before you sign. The deposit and the months before opening are calculated from it. Shared kitchens charge roughly 15-45 per hour (The Food Corridor, 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey): multiply by your prep hours (sofrito, stock, cleaning the seafood) and add storage. A permitted commissary is required: paella for clients cannot be prepped in a home kitchen, and cottage food rules do not cover it. Get quotes in your area before you sign.
c0046: Water, electricity and phone that the commissary fee does not cover. Propane (and wood where a permit allows it) is not here: it scales with your events and lives in the disposables and cooking fuel row above. It is the one cell for this cost, so you change it in one place and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0048: General liability or a BOP that does NOT exclude open flame at events (venues and planners often require 1M per occurrence), commercial auto for the van, workers' comp for your W-2 staff and inland marine for the pans and burners. Venues ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured. Add liquor liability only if the client supplies alcohol and your staff serves it. Insureon publishes averages for small businesses (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab); the example is a Kit estimate, so get quotes from an insurance agent. It is counted once, as an annual expense, not also in startup costs.
c0050: Extra seafood on the day, ice, lemons and parking at the venue: the unbudgeted costs of each event. It is a VARIABLE cost: it rises and falls with the number of events, so it cannot sit among the fixed costs or it would move the break-even without anyone noticing. Fuel is not here: van fuel has its own fixed line on the "3-Year P&L" tab, and cooking propane is in the disposables row.
c0055: Principal requested: bank or SBA 7(a). The example loan is above the $50,000 ceiling of the SBA Microloan, so it fits an SBA 7(a) loan or a secured bank loan. If your loan is an SBA 7(a), this is the cell. It is the only loan that the amortization schedule, the P&L interest and the DSCR use. The "Financing" tab checks that the sources of funds match the total cash needed on the "Startup Costs" tab (which includes working capital and the burner, pan, van and fit-out contingency): copy the loan suggested there into this cell until the difference reaches zero. A lender will ask for your plan and projections.
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example (10%) is the kit's assumption for an SBA 7(a) loan. A smaller loan secured by a used van and kitchen equipment often prices above a storefront loan: ask two lenders for quotes, and ask about SBA-guaranteed loans, before you set it.
c0059: Total years, interest-only period included. A used van, burners and pans lose value faster than a storefront build-out, so the term is shorter. SBA 7(a) allows up to 10 years for equipment and working capital.
c0079: The paella burners and stands, the paella pans, the used cargo van and its upfit, and the fire marshal or propane setup inspection: the cooking assets and the vehicle are depreciated together. Straight-line book depreciation; tax methods such as MACRS or Section 179 are separate, so confirm with your accountant.
c0081: The propane and fire-safety kit, commissary fit-out, software, smallwares and paella tools, and event setup and holding equipment. Loading and unloading at every event wears them faster than a fixed kitchen, so a short life is prudent. Straight-line book depreciation; MACRS or Section 179 are tax treatments: confirm with your accountant.
c0087: INFORMATION ONLY: it does not enter any calculation in this workbook. It is your estimate of the most events a year your crew can handle with one van and a second paella chef; two events on the same Saturday is the practical limit, and Saturdays in May, June and October are the bottleneck. Compare it with the events per year you plan and with the optimistic scenario: if the plan goes above it, you need a second set of pans and burners or more staff. Volume itself is driven by the "Events per year" cell above.
c0089: A new caterer does not book in month one what it books in month eight: weddings are reserved months ahead and corporate clients want to try your paella first. Events per year above is the year-1 AVERAGE: the ramp only spreads year 1's sales across the months (slower start, stronger finish) and keeps the annual total. At 100% there is no ramp.
c0093: Getting the commissary agreement, the permits and the van ready takes weeks, and your test paellas for each pan size happen before your first booking, so you pay commissary rent before you earn anything. It belongs in startup costs, not in the P&L.
c0095: Calculated by formula on the burner and stand, paella pan, used van, van upfit and fire / propane inspection lines: if you change the van price, the contingency recalculates on its own. The note on that row of the "Startup Costs" tab lists exactly which lines are included.
c0098: Average days between the event and the money in your bank. Private clients usually pay a deposit when they book the date (caterers commonly ask for 25-50%: Kit estimate) and the balance before the event, and many companies pay at 30 days, so the example sits in between. Raise it if clients or marketplaces pay later. The workbook does not model deposits: they improve your real cash flow.
c0106: ZERO by default: a paella caterer sells no alcohol. Sangria goes out without alcohol, or with wine the client buys, at no margin. If the client supplies alcohol, a licensed service should pour it under its own insurance. Selling alcohol requires a liquor license (and, in some states, an event-by-event caterer's permit): check your state before adding it. Keep liquor liability coverage whenever your staff pours at your events.
c0144: Four 3-ring paella burners with legs (an XL 3-ring burner with tripod and regulator for pans up to 36 in (90 cm) runs about 549: Kit estimate from store prices), a rolling stand (about 399 for a 2-ring one) and wind guards. Get quotes before you buy.
c0147: Paella pans by size: 2 × 36 in (90 cm), about 40 guests each; 3 × 32 in (80 cm), about 30; 3 × 26 in (65 cm), about 18 (Kit estimate). A 36 in pan runs about 349 (store price, Kit estimate). Carbon steel or enameled. They are depreciated with the burners.
c0149: Propane and fire-safety kit: eight 20-lb cylinders (about 4.7 gallons or 18 liters each), regulators, hoses within their date, two fire extinguishers (your fire marshal says which ones) and a fire blanket.
c0151: Commissary prep fit-out: shelving, sheet pans and labeled tubs for sofrito and stock. Ask the kitchen what it already provides before you budget this line.
c0153: A used cargo van that carries the pans, burners, cylinders and coolers. It is not refrigerated: raw seafood travels in coolers with ice at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, and drop-off paella in insulated carriers at 135 °F (57 °C) or above. Prices vary with size, mileage and condition, so get several quotes. A Transit-size van does not need a CDL (that starts at 26,001 lb GVWR).
c0155: Shelving, upright cylinder racks with ventilation, tie-downs for the pans and burners, and the vehicle wrap. Check that your insurance covers the upfit.
c0157: State filing fees for the LLC (Secretary of State) plus an attorney's review of your standard contract (deposit, cancellation tiers, final headcount, a plan B for wind and rain, and an unauthorized open-flame clause) or a filing service; a registered agent is also needed. Fees vary a lot by state. The "Taxable / recoverable tax?" column is set to No: it only matters if you enter a recoverable input tax rate (for example UK VAT).
c0160: Varies a lot by city, county and state: get the amounts for yours before you close the budget. Expect the catering or health permit, temporary event permits, the business license, the sales tax permit, ServSafe Manager and food handler cards.
c0162: Only if your city or the venue requires them: a fire marshal or event permit and an inspection of your propane setup. Rules vary by county and fire district, so ask your fire marshal. If nobody asks for it, enter 0.
c0164: Catering software for proposals, e-signature contracts, deposits and final balances, plus a card reader and a tablet.
c0166: Paddles, ladles, knives, color-coded cutting boards, hotel pans, calibrated probe thermometers and heat-resistant gloves: the tools that get depreciated. Daily disposables are NOT depreciated: they go in the disposables and cooking fuel line of the P&L, at the % of sales set in the "0. Assumptions" tab.
c0168: Bomba rice, saffron, stock base, seafood and chicken for your test paellas, and disposables for your first events. With 0% recoverable input tax (the US default), any sales tax you pay on this purchase is treated as a cost.
c0170: Website, photos and video of paella cooked live, listings on The Knot, WeddingWire, Zola and ezCater, Google Business Profile and your first bridal show.
c0172: Event setup and holding: a cooking tent for the paella area (set apart from the guest tent), folding tables, a handwashing station (San Diego County asks for a 5-gallon one, 19 liters: check your county), coolers for the seafood, six chafing dishes for the tapas and insulated carriers for the drop-offs.
c0180: What you buy: burners and pans, the van and its upfit, the propane kit, event setup, launch and formation costs. The cash cushion is not an investment: it is working capital.
c0205: Sales of paella packages: the live-cooked paella with salad and bread, plus the paella chef and the staff who serve it, across drop-offs, backyard paella parties, corporate events, weddings and premium seafood events. All of it carries cost of goods sold at the paella package rate.
c0207: Sales of add-ons: tapas hour, desserts, non-alcoholic sangria and drinks, rentals, extra hours and travel fees. The client buys any alcohol separately, so there is no alcohol revenue.
c0221: The monthly amount is typed in "0. Assumptions"; here it is multiplied by twelve. It covers your commissary hours, storage and the space for the pans and burners, not storefront rent. The months before opening are on the "Startup Costs" tab and are NOT counted twice.
c0225: Water, electricity and phone that the commissary fee does not cover. No propane or wood here: they scale with your events and sit in the disposables and cooking fuel line.
c0235: Licensed hauler for trash, used oil and shells. Ask the commissary first: many include removal in the fee. If yours does not, get a quote in your area.
c0237: Replacement of paella pans (they warp), burners (clogged rings), regulators and hoses (they expire).
c0239: ServSafe Manager (Certified Food Protection Manager) and food handler cards for you and your team, plus their renewals. The required cards vary by state.
c0241: Food cost and labor for the tastings you offer couples, planners and companies (a small paella cooked live). Many caterers charge a fee and credit it toward the booking: if you do, lower this line.
c0268: Ceiling for cost of goods (disposables and cooking fuel have their own line): kit benchmark (editable estimate), based on the 28-35% food cost range for caterers in the benchmarks table.
c0270: Ceiling: kit benchmark (editable estimate), above the 25-35% labor range that pricing guides report because it includes the owner's own pay as paella chef.
c0272: There is no storefront rent in this workbook: 7% is a prudent ceiling for the commissary kitchen and equipment storage, a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A business with its own fixed kitchen carries a much higher occupancy cost.
c0344: Sells, runs the tastings, plans menus and cooks the paella at the events. Covers the main shift at every event. The rest of the owner's pay comes from profit.
c0346: Lead cook / second paella chef, part-time W-2: runs the second paella at big events and the second event on a Saturday. One paella chef can run about three pans at once. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE, between the mean and the 75th percentile for restaurant cooks (BLS OEWS, May 2025).
c0348: Servers and buffet attendants hired per event and paid hourly as W-2 employees, about one team member per 25 guests (miamigrillcatering.com). Their FTE is a fraction because they only work event hours. Treating them as 1099 contractors is a misclassification risk (FLSA; California AB5). Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE. The voluntary gratuity is theirs.
c0350: Part-time W-2 prep cook and driver: makes the sofrito and stock and cleans the seafood in the commissary, loads the van and drives to venues. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0364: Hours of work per person for one event: prep, loading, travel, arriving two to three hours early, setup, about one hour of cooking, about two hours of service, and breakdown and cleanup. Serving is only part of it. Hours × people × events per year sets the event staff cost.
c0366: Average number of people working each event: 1 on a drop-off, 2 at a backyard paella party, 3 at a company event, 4.5 at a wedding and 4 at a premium seafood event (Kit estimate). Weighted by the example mix in the Word plan, that averages about 2.5. Raise it for bigger events: the staffing sizes itself.
c0379: 1. "0. Assumptions" is the control sheet: events per year, price per guest excl. sales tax, guests per event, the mix of paella packages and add-ons, cost of goods sold, commissary and equipment storage, financing and taxes.
c0421: A monthly commissary cost (hours + storage) and space for the pans and burners, plus a deposit and rent for the months before opening
c0422: Paella for clients has to be prepped in a permitted kitchen, not at home, so a commissary or shared kitchen is a real recurring cost. Leaving it out makes the business look like it has no occupancy cost.
c0429: Two useful lives: the burners, pans, van and its upfits on one, and the propane kit, the setup and the equipment on the other. The Startup Costs tab calculates the annual charge.
c0430: The burners, pans and van wear out at a different speed than the propane kit, the setup and the equipment. Working capital, opening inventory and launch marketing are not fixed assets, so they are not depreciated.
c0431: Van and equipment insurance, and liability
c0435: Propane (and wood where a permit allows it)
c0437: Included in the disposables and cooking fuel line
c0438: Propane (and wood where a permit allows it) scales with the pans you cook and the number of events: here it lives in one percentage of sales, and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0441: A percentage calculated on the burner, pan, van and upfit lines
c0442: If you change the van price, the contingency recalculates instead of staying at the old amount.
c0461: A percentage of sales, treated as a variable cost; van fuel has its own fixed line
c0462: Extra seafood, ice, lemons and venue parking rise and fall with the number of events: among the fixed costs they would distort the break-even.
c0465: Every sale carries its cost of goods: paella packages and add-ons each at their own rate
c0479: Paella cooked live with salad and bread. The low end is a per-plate price at one operator (zola.com); $26-31 per person is the usual range at tasteofpaella.com, and lobster paella is the premium. Your price per guest runs higher because it includes the paella chef and the staff.
c0480: Spanish menu with staff, per person
c0483: Full Spanish menu with service staff: from $44 per person (zola.com) to $65, stepping down to $53 by tier (miamigrillcatering.com). In weddings, couples usually spend about $50 per person (weddingwire.com).
c0487: Bomba rice, uncooked, per guest. Add 10-15% for large groups and plan 2-3 times the rice volume in stock. Weigh it again for every quote.
c0493: 36 in (90 cm): about 40 · 32 in (80 cm): about 30 · 26 in (65 cm): about 18
c0495: Servings of a full paella with salad and bread. Size the pans from the guest count, and keep each pan within what one burner heats evenly: a good socarrat needs even heat across the whole pan.
c0499: Caterer food cost as a share of the price. Seafood prices swing, so re-cost every quote and test the result at the top of the range.
c0501: 36 in pan about $349 · XL 3-ring burner about $549
c0503: Store prices, not verified quotes. The XL 3-ring burner comes with tripod and regulator for pans up to 36 in (90 cm); a 2-ring rolling stand is about $399, and renting a 36 in pan about $39.90. Get current quotes.
c0508: Paella chef and attendant billed separately
c0511: One operator bills the paella chef ($300 for 2 hours), a buffet attendant ($190 for 2 hours), dishes and flatware ($5-10 per person) and a $1,250 minimum on top of the food. Your price per guest already includes the paella chef and the staff, so compare like with like.
c0515: Mean hourly wages for restaurant cooks (35-2014) and nonrestaurant food servers (35-3041), and the median for chefs and head cooks (35-1011); 75th percentile $21.45 for cooks and $18.51 for servers. The plan pays the second paella chef between the mean and the 75th percentile for cooks, and the owner's pay comes from profit, below the chefs and head cooks median.
c0519: 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey; 42% of operators charge $20-$29 per hour. Storage costs extra, and not every kitchen lets you keep burners and propane cylinders on site.
c0523: Operators set a minimum guest count for cooking on site (20, or 25 in peak season, at tasteofpaella.com; 30 for live cooking at Viton Paella on zola.com) and a minimum spend (from $500 to $1,600 across the operators on zola.com). Set your own and state it in every proposal.
c0529: 6-8 lb (2.7-3.6 kg) of propane · 1 team member per 25 guests
c0531: About 6-8 lb of propane (about $10-15) for a 60-guest event, plus disposables at about $0.75 per guest (Kit estimate). Staffing: about one team member per 25 guests (miamigrillcatering.com).
c0597: The same calculation on what you BUY (burners and pans, van, upfits, propane kit, event setup, launch and formation costs), without working capital: that money is not spent, it is tied up and comes back when the business closes. For reference only: the payback that matters is the one above
